entities.summary:
The concept of a dwarf planet, formalized by the International Astronomical Union (IAU) in August 2006, fundamentally redefined our understanding of the Solar System's architecture, distinguishing it from the classical planets and smaller bodies. This classification applies to celestial objects that orbit the Sun, possess sufficient mass to achieve hydrostatic equilibrium (making them nearly round), but have not gravitationally cleared their orbital neighborhood of other debris. Its significance lies in providing a more nuanced framework for categorizing the diverse array of planetary-mass objects discovered beyond Neptune, profoundly influencing planetary science, astrobiology, and public perception of the cosmos.

The genesis of this definition stemmed from a growing crisis in planetary classification, precipitated by the discovery of numerous large trans-Neptunian objects, most notably Eris in 2005. Eris, initially thought to be larger than Pluto, forced astronomers to confront the inadequacy of the existing, informal definition of a planet. The contentious 2006 IAU General Assembly in Prague ultimately passed Resolution 5A, which established three categories of Solar System bodies: 'planets,' 'dwarf planets,' and 'small Solar System bodies.' This resolution famously led to the reclassification of Pluto, which had been considered the ninth planet since its discovery in 1930, as a dwarf planet alongside Ceres, Haumea, Makemake, and Eris.
